turns.doctor_question: Hello, it’s nice to meet you. What brings you in today?
turns.patient_response:
Nice to meet you too. Well, I'm here because I just can't stop focusing on my face. There's this... this rough, sunken-looking patch on it. Every time I look in the mirror or see a picture of myself, it's all I can see. It just makes one side of me look real old and beat-up. 

It's really getting to me, to be honest. The thing is, my family and other people keep saying they barely notice anything at all, but... I just can't stop seeing it.

symptom_reasoning.S067: The patient describes an intense preoccupation with a perceived rough, sunken patch on their face that others state they barely notice at all.

turns.doctor_question: How convinced are you that the patch is as severe and noticeable as it seems to you, despite what others tell you?
turns.patient_response:
Well, I'm... I'm pretty convinced. I mean, I hear what my family is saying, and sometimes I try to tell myself that maybe they're right and it's not as bad as I think. But then I look in the mirror and... it's just right there. 

It's plain as day to me. I don't know if they're just trying to be nice or if they really don't see it, but I know what I'm looking at. So, yeah, I'm very convinced it looks bad, no matter what they tell me.

turns.doctor_question: When you become focused on the patch, do you feel driven to repeatedly check it in the mirror or try to hide or fix it to reduce your distress?
turns.patient_response:
Yeah, I do. It's... it's a whole routine, really. Before I head out to the job site, or even if I'm just going over to my sister's place for her game night, I end up in the bathroom checking the mirror. I'll just stand there, turning my head this way and that, trying to see how the light hits it. 

I catch myself rubbing at the spot, too, like maybe I can smooth it out or something. If I feel like it's looking really bad that day, I'll pull my work hat down real low to try and cover it up. And honestly... sometimes if I think it's just too obvious, I'll just make up an excuse and not go out at all.

symptom_reasoning.S068: The patient describes repetitive behaviors performed in response to perceived appearance flaws, including repeatedly checking the mirror under different lighting, rubbing at the spot, and camouflaging with a hat.

turns.doctor_question: Do you ever think your concern about the patch might be excessive or mistaken, or are you completely certain that it looks as severe as you believe?
turns.patient_response: I guess... I don't really know. Like I said before, I hear what people are telling me, and a small part of me wonders if maybe I am making a bigger deal out of it than I should. But then I look in the mirror, and I'm just certain it looks terrible. So, I don't know if I'd say I'm completely certain I'm right, but I'm definitely not convinced I'm wrong, either. It just is what it is when I look at it.

turns.doctor_question: When you check the patch repeatedly, does it feel like you’re trying to relieve an unwanted thought that you recognize as excessive, or are you mainly inspecting a flaw that you genuinely believe is visibly severe?
turns.patient_response:
Well, I'm not sure I quite get what you mean by relieving a thought. It doesn't really feel like that. 

I mean... I'm just checking it because it's there, and it looks bad to me. I'm looking in the mirror to see how noticeable it is, or trying to see if maybe it doesn't look quite as severe today. So I guess it's more of that second thing you said. I genuinely believe it looks terrible, and I'm just inspecting it because of that. It doesn't feel like just some thought in my head I'm trying to get rid of... it feels like a real physical thing I'm looking at.

symptom_reasoning.S067: The patient expresses a strong belief and concern that their physical flaw looks severe and terrible, confirming a preoccupation with a perceived physical defect.
symptom_reasoning.S068: The patient explicitly confirms engaging in repetitive behaviors by frequently looking in the mirror to check and inspect the noticeable severity of the flaw.

turns.doctor_question: How long have you been preoccupied with this patch on your face?
turns.patient_response: It's been a while now. I'd say... probably around two or three years that it's really been bothering me like this. It kind of just started out as something I noticed, and then over time, it just became this thing I can't stop focusing on.

symptom_reasoning.S067: The patient describes that the patch on their face has been bothering them for two to three years and has become something they cannot stop focusing on, confirming preoccupation with a perceived appearance flaw.
